title: At a Restaurant
pronunciation_focus_summary: The uvular R -- the signature French sound. Found in restaurant, garcon, addition, and dozens of essential dining words. Produced in the back of the throat as a gentle uvular fricative, not with the tongue tip like English R.

phrases.text: Je voudrais une table pour deux, s'il vous plait
phrases.translation: I would like a table for two, please
phrases.phonetic_ipa: ʒə vudʁɛ yn tabl puʁ dø sil vu plɛ
phrases.phonetic_approx: zhuh voo-DREH oon TAH-bluh poor DUH seel voo PLEH
phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'r' in 'voudrais' and 'pour' is the uvular R -- a soft friction in the back of the throat. 'Deux' has the closed 'eu' sound -- round your lips tightly. The final 't' in 'plait' is silent.
phrases.example_sentence: Bonsoir, je voudrais une table pour deux, s'il vous plait.

phrases.translation: I would like to reserve a table
phrases.pronunciation_notes: Three French R sounds in this phrase -- excellent practice for the uvular R. 'Reserver' starts with R, has one in the middle, and 'voudrais' has another. The '-er' ending sounds like 'ay'.
phrases.example_sentence: Je voudrais reserver une table pour ce soir a vingt heures.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'r' in 'carte' is the uvular R followed by a 't' -- practice this R-T transition. The final 'e' of 'carte' is barely pronounced. 'La carte' is the full list of dishes; 'le menu' is a fixed-price set meal.
phrases.example_sentence: Est-ce que je peux voir la carte, s'il vous plait ?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: In French, 'menu' refers to a fixed-price set meal, not the full list of dishes. The 'u' in 'menu' is the tight French U -- lips rounded forward, tongue toward the front of the mouth.
phrases.example_sentence: Bonjour, le menu du jour, s'il vous plait.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: A useful long phrase that flows naturally. The 'r' in 'recommandez' is uvular. The nasal 'an' in '-mandez' sounds like 'ahn' with air through the nose. The final '-ez' sounds like 'ay'.
phrases.example_sentence: Tout a l'air delicieux. Qu'est-ce que vous recommandez ?

phrases.text: Je prends le plat du jour
phrases.translation: I'll have the dish of the day
phrases.phonetic_ipa: ʒə pʁɑ̃ lə pla dy ʒuʁ
phrases.phonetic_approx: zhuh PRAHN luh PLAH doo ZHOOR
phrases.pronunciation_notes: 'Prends' has a nasal 'an' vowel and a silent 'ds' at the end. The 'r' is uvular. 'Plat' has a silent final 't'. 'Jour' ends with the French R. 'Je prends' is used for ordering -- literally 'I take'.
phrases.example_sentence: Je prends le plat du jour et une carafe d'eau.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: False friend alert! In French, 'entree' means STARTER, not main course as in American English. The 'en' is a nasal vowel 'ahn'. The 'r' is uvular. The final '-ee' is a clear 'ay' sound.
phrases.example_sentence: Comme entree, je voudrais la soupe a l'oignon.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The nasal 'in' in 'principal' sounds like 'ehn'. 'Plat' has a silent final 't'. The French R appears in 'principal'. The final 'l' is clearly pronounced.
phrases.example_sentence: Pour le plat principal, je voudrais le poulet roti.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Unlike English, stress falls on the last syllable. The final 't' is silent. The 'r' before the silent 't' is the uvular R. Both 's' letters are pronounced as 's' (not 'z').
phrases.example_sentence: Qu'est-ce que vous avez comme dessert ?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: This is how you order free tap water in France -- essential knowledge! 'Carafe' has two uvular R sounds, making it excellent practice. The 'eau' sounds like 'oh'. The 'f' in 'carafe' is pronounced.
phrases.example_sentence: Une carafe d'eau pour la table, s'il vous plait.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The nasal 'in' in 'vin' does not pronounce the 'n' -- just nasalize the vowel. 'Rouge' starts with the uvular R and ends with the 'zh' sound (like the 's' in 'measure'). The 'e' at the end is silent.
phrases.example_sentence: Un verre de vin rouge, s'il vous plait.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Two different nasal vowels back to back: 'vin' uses the 'in' nasal (more forward, like 'ehn') and 'blanc' uses the 'an' nasal (more open, like 'ahn'). The final 'c' in 'blanc' is silent.
phrases.example_sentence: Qu'est-ce que vous avez comme vin blanc ?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The '-tion' in French is pronounced 'syohn' with a nasal vowel -- never 'shun' as in English. The double 'd' is pronounced as a single 'd'. In France, the waiter will never bring the check unless you ask.
phrases.example_sentence: Excusez-moi, l'addition, s'il vous plait.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The ending '-ien' is a nasal vowel. For feminine, add '-ne': 'vegetarienne' (vay-zhay-tah-RYENN), which denasalizes the vowel. The 'r' in 'vegetarien' is uvular. The 'g' before 'e' is soft ('zh').
phrases.example_sentence: Excusez-moi, je suis vegetarien. Qu'est-ce que vous proposez ?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The final '-eux' has the closed 'eu' sound -- round your lips as if whistling and say 'uh'. The 'c' in 'c'est' sounds like 's'. A wonderful compliment to give your server or host.
phrases.example_sentence: C'est delicieux ! Mes compliments au chef.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Critical safety phrase. Liaison: the 's' in 'suis' links to the vowel in 'allergique' as a 'z' sound. Two French R sounds. The 'g' before 'i' is soft ('zh'). Common completions: aux noix (nuts), aux fruits de mer (seafood), au gluten (gluten).
phrases.example_sentence: Attention, je suis allergique aux noix. Est-ce qu'il y en a dans ce plat ?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'on' in 'bon' is a nasal vowel -- air through the nose. The 'e' in 'tres' is the open E sound. The French R in 'tres' comes right after the 't'. Short and effective compliment.
phrases.example_sentence: C'est tres bon ! Mes compliments au chef.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Liaison: 'bon' links to 'appetit' -- the 'n' connects to the 'a'. The final 't' in 'appetit' is actually pronounced here, which is an exception to the usual silent final consonant rule in French.
phrases.example_sentence: Voila vos plats. Bon appetit !

phrases.text: Est-ce que je peux avoir du pain ?
phrases.phonetic_ipa: ɛs kə ʒə pø avwaʁ dy pɛ̃
phrases.phonetic_approx: ess kuh zhuh PUH ah-VWAHR doo PEHN
phrases.pronunciation_notes: Bread is free and unlimited in French restaurants -- just ask! 'Pain' has the nasal 'ain' vowel. 'Avoir' ends with the uvular R. 'Peux' has the closed 'eu' sound -- lips forward and rounded.
phrases.example_sentence: Excusez-moi, est-ce que je peux avoir du pain, s'il vous plait ?

phrases.translation: I would like to pay by card
phrases.pronunciation_notes: Both 'par' and 'carte' contain the uvular R. 'Payer' has a subtle 'y' glide between syllables. Card payment is widely accepted in France, but some small bistros may be cash only.
phrases.example_sentence: L'addition, s'il vous plait. Je voudrais payer par carte.

dialogues.context: Arriving at a restaurant without a reservation

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Bonsoir, je voudrais une table pour deux, s'il vous plait.
exchanges.translation: Good evening, I would like a table for two, please.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: bohn-SWAHR zhuh voo-DREH oon TAH-bluh poor DUH seel voo PLEH

exchanges.speaker: waiter
exchanges.translation: Good evening! Do you have a reservation?

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Non, je n'ai pas reserve. C'est possible ?
exchanges.translation: No, I didn't make a reservation. Is it possible?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: nohn zhuh NAY pah ray-zehr-VAY. seh poh-SEE-bluh

exchanges.speaker: waiter
exchanges.text: Pas de probleme. Suivez-moi, j'ai une table pres de la fenetre.
exchanges.translation: No problem. Follow me, I have a table near the window.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: pah duh proh-BLEM. swee-VAY mwah zhay oon TAH-bluh preh duh lah fuh-NEH-truh

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Merci beaucoup. La carte, s'il vous plait.
exchanges.translation: Thank you very much. The menu, please.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: mehr-SEE boh-KOO. lah KAHRT seel voo PLEH

dialogues.notes: In popular Parisian restaurants, reservations are strongly recommended for dinner. For lunch, walk-ins are usually easier. Always say 'Bonsoir' (not 'Bonjour') when arriving for dinner.

dialogues.context: Ordering a full meal with drinks

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Oui. Comme entree, je prends la soupe a l'oignon.
exchanges.translation: Yes. For the starter, I'll have the onion soup.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: wee. kohm ahn-TRAY zhuh PRAHN lah SOOP ah loh-NYOHN

exchanges.speaker: waiter
exchanges.text: Tres bien. Et comme plat principal ?
exchanges.translation: Very good. And for the main course?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: treh BYEHN. ay kohm PLAH prehn-see-PAL

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Le boeuf bourguignon, s'il vous plait.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: luh BUFF boor-gee-NYOHN seel voo PLEH

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Un verre de vin rouge et une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plait.
exchanges.translation: A glass of red wine and a carafe of water, please.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: uhn VEHR duh VEHN ROOZH ay oon kah-RAHF DOH seel voo PLEH

exchanges.speaker: waiter
exchanges.text: Parfait. Je vous apporte ca tout de suite.
exchanges.translation: Perfect. I'll bring that right away.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: pahr-FEH. zhuh vooz ah-POHRT sah too duh SWEET

dialogues.notes: French meals traditionally have three courses: entree (starter), plat principal (main), and dessert. Ordering just a main course is perfectly acceptable, especially at lunch. 'Je prends' (I'll take) is the standard way to order.

dialogues.context: Dealing with dietary restrictions and asking for the check

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Excusez-moi, je suis allergique aux noix. Ce plat en contient ?
exchanges.translation: Excuse me, I'm allergic to nuts. Does this dish contain any?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: ex-koo-ZAY mwah zhuh SWEEZ ah-lehr-ZHEEK oh NWAH. suh PLAH ahn kohn-TYEHN

exchanges.speaker: waiter
exchanges.text: Je vais verifier avec le chef. Un instant, s'il vous plait.
exchanges.translation: I'll check with the chef. One moment, please.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: zhuh VAY vay-ree-FYAY ah-VEK luh SHEF. uhn ehn-STAHN seel voo PLEH

exchanges.speaker: waiter
exchanges.text: Non, il n'y a pas de noix dans ce plat. Vous pouvez le prendre sans probleme.
exchanges.translation: No, there are no nuts in this dish. You can have it without any problem.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: nohn eel NYAH pah duh NWAH dahn suh PLAH. voo poo-VAY luh PRAHN-druh sahn proh-BLEM

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Merci beaucoup. C'etait delicieux. L'addition, s'il vous plait.
exchanges.translation: Thank you very much. That was delicious. The check, please.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: mehr-SEE boh-KOO. say-TEH day-lee-SYUH. lah-dee-SYOHN seel voo PLEH

exchanges.speaker: waiter
exchanges.text: Voila. Vous payez par carte ou en especes ?
exchanges.translation: Here you go. Are you paying by card or cash?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: vwah-LAH. voo pay-YAY pahr KAHRT oo ahn ess-PESS

dialogues.notes: Always mention allergies clearly -- French waiters take this seriously. The phrase 'Est-ce qu'il y a des noix/du gluten/des fruits de mer dans ce plat ?' is very useful. Service (tip) is included in the price by law, but leaving 1-2 euros for good service is appreciated.

cultural_notes.title: French restaurant etiquette -- the art of dining
cultural_notes.content: Dining in France is a cultural ritual, not just eating. Meals are meant to be savored slowly -- lunch can last 1-2 hours, dinner even longer. The waiter will never bring the check until you ask; being left alone is a sign of respect, not neglect. Always say 'Bonjour' (or 'Bonsoir' for dinner) when entering and 'Au revoir' when leaving. Bread goes directly on the table, not on your plate. Keep your hands visible above the table (not in your lap -- unlike American custom). Service is included in the price ('service compris'), so tipping is optional, but rounding up or leaving 1-2 euros for excellent service is a kind gesture.

cultural_notes.title: Menu vs La carte -- a common confusion
cultural_notes.content: In France, 'le menu' refers to a fixed-price set meal (also called 'le menu du jour' or 'la formule'), typically offering a choice of starter + main or main + dessert at a set price. If you want to see the full list of available dishes and order individually, ask for 'la carte'. This is the opposite of how English uses the word 'menu'. Set menus are usually a great value and an excellent way to try the chef's specialties. Most restaurants display their menu and prices outside the door, so you can browse before deciding to enter.
